title: The messy politics behind Google’s big AI shakeup
excerpt: Google’s AI leadership changes — such as Demis Hassabis’ role change and Jeff Dean’s departure — may have come down to pressure to speed up products and internal ethical conflicts.
content_html:
In the AI industry, Google prides itself on seeming like the adult in the room: quiet, stable, time-tested. On Wednesday, even as the company announced its largest AI org shakeup yet, Google and its leaders presented a unified front, keeping their messaging focused on how the changes tee up future success.

But the reality is that the laundry list of executive changes likely signal deeper issues within Google’s AI organization. That starts with its tenuous position in the AI race, and it stretches to problems like Google DeepMind leader Demis Hassabis’ interest in longer-term research over shorter-term product shipping, as well as bubbling political opposition from top employees like DeepMind chief scientist Jeff Dean.

A current Google employee, who requested anonymity due to fear of retaliation, said one of the changes — Dean’s departure — is an example of “the vestiges of Google’s idealism” fully dying out. “Losing Jeff continues the brain drain at Google,” they said. “Mediocrity is the likely result.”

Wednesday’s news rocked the AI industry, which is difficult to do during an era when AI researchers are constantly switching between roles and labs like a game of musical chairs. Google announced that Demis Hassabis is stepping away from DeepMind’s day-to-day operations to focus on AGI and research; Koray Kavukcuoglu, DeepMind’s current CTO, will step up to lead DeepMind in Hassabis’ place. At the same time, Jeff Dean, a 27-year Google veteran and the company’s 30th employee, will leave the organization alongside three top Google AI researchers to form a new AI startup.

“Losing Jeff continues the brain drain at Google. Mediocrity is the likely result.”

Google is widely viewed as being the most successful of the established tech giants in the AI race, far surpassing progress by Meta, Amazon, and Apple. But Google is still viewed as slower-moving than OpenAI and Anthropic, and it certainly hasn’t lapped them in frontier models. Both Hassabis and Google CEO Sundar Pichai made that point in their statements.

“We are committed to being at the frontier, and are super focused on the areas where we need to improve,” Pichai wrote, adding, “We have to continue to move fast and with clear purpose here.” Hassabis wrote that the company is entering a “next chapter” and that it has “all the ingredients to lead from here, and I firmly believe we will.”

Key figures in the AI industry seemed to view the changes as Hassabis stepping to the side in favor of a faster-moving, product-focused push at GDM.

“There’s been far more internal competition at Google than I’ve seen in the last decade primarily around the AI product space,” one former Google employee, who recently left the company and had knowledge of Google’s AI operations, told The Verge. They added that there’s been pressure to hire more employees who can speed up launches of more products, in keeping with the intensifying competition.

“There’s been far more internal competition at Google than I’ve seen in the last decade primarily around the AI product space.”

Another source within the AI industry, who requested anonymity due to ongoing work with AI labs, said, “I agree with everyone’s read that this is a sign of Demis’ loss of influence.”

Hassabis hasn’t been quiet in sharing that his interests lie in the scientific advancements that could come from AI, perhaps more so than the commercialization of the technology. Pichai wrote in a blog post that Hassabis’ next move will focus on “actively shaping the future of AGI” as DeepMind chair and Alphabet’s chief scientist, while continuing his role leading the drug-discovery spinoff Isomorphic Labs.

But AI leadership is only one of the problems facing Google — and industry insiders The Verge spoke with kept coming back to one main question: How much of this had to do with increasing ethical conflicts within Google itself?

A contributing factor to both Hassabis’s role change and Dean’s departure may have been Google’s deal with the Department of Defense, Tyler Johnston, founder of the nonprofit AI industry watchdog The Midas Project, told The Verge. That deal could potentially allow for the use of Google AI in mass surveillance and lethal autonomous weapons.

“This has already caused staff departures and a unionization effort at DeepMind,” Johnston said. “There are many signs suggesting Dean and Hassabis may have personally felt opposed. In fact, DeepMind was initially acquired by Google with an agreement not to sell the technology for military or intelligence purposes.”

Zvi Mowshowitz, a blogger followed closely by AI researchers, echoed that Dean’s decision to leave could potentially be “related to Google’s decisions on the DoW contract.”

“DeepMind was initially acquired by Google with an agreement not to sell the technology for military or intelligence purposes.”

Dean is leaving to launch Discovery Loop, an AI startup that aims to automate thousands of science and engineering experiments in areas like drug discovery, hardware design, clean energy, and material design. Joining him as cofounders are three additional top Google AI researchers: Sanjay Ghemawat, Quoc Le, and Oriol Vinyals.

“Losing Jeff feels like a blow for morality and basic human decency within Google,” the current Google employee said. “He was one of the few remaining visible, powerful figures here who was willing to speak out on moral issues such as ICE agents executing American citizens, AI surveillance, and autonomous lethal weapons.”

Dean was one of the most high-profile dissenters to the Department of Defense’s labeling of Anthropic as a supply chain risk after the company stood firm on its red lines for military use of its AI. In March, Dean was one of dozens of tech industry leaders and employees to file an amicus brief in support of Anthropic’s lawsuit, laying out concerns over the Trump administration’s decision — as well as about AI’s risks and implications. (He also pushed back on the Trump administration in January, saying that ICE’s killing of Alex Pretti was “absolutely shameful” and that “every person regardless of political affiliation should be denouncing this.”)

Jeff Dean had publicly disavowed both the same red lines as Anthropic in the past.

In April, after Anthropic’s drawn-out fight with the DoD over its red lines — prohibiting domestic mass surveillance and lethal autonomous weapons (with no human in the loop) — Google became one of the companies to happily fill the gap left by Anthropic’s Pentagon blacklisting. Like a handful of other companies, Google signed on to allow the Pentagon to use its AI for “any lawful use.”

Dean had publicly disavowed both the same red lines in the past. In February, he wrote on X, “Mass surveillance violates the Fourth Amendment and has a chilling effect on freedom of expression. Surveillance systems are prone to misuse for political or discriminatory purposes.” And in 2018, both Dean and Hassabis signed a public pledge disavowing lethal autonomous weapons: “We the undersigned agree that the decision to take a human life should never be delegated to a machine.”

Alex Turner, a Google researcher who quit over the company’s Pentagon deal, wrote in an op-ed last month that Dean’s “departure would be a disaster for the company” and that “by signing [the amicus brief], he broke from the company line, which probably made things awkward within the C-suite.”

In the amicus brief that Dean signed earlier this year, the group wrote, “We build, train, and study the large-scale AI systems that serve a wide range of users and deployments, including in the consequential domains of national security, law enforcement, and military operations.” The group described itself as “professionals with direct knowledge of what these systems can and cannot do, and what is at stake when their deployment outpaces the legal and ethical frameworks designed to govern them.”

Dean’s departure may remove a high-profile critic, but it certainly won’t dispel criticism within the organization as a whole. Since the beginning of the year, an increasing number of Google employees have expressed discontent with the organization’s politics.

“Sergey [Brin] did a 180 politically, Sundar stood behind Trump at his inauguration,” the current Google employee said. “Now one of the only remaining figures at the company willing to speak out on moral issues is gone. Who knows what we will sell out next?”

blocks.html_en: • Hayden Field

sentences.en: Hayden Field
sentences.zh: 海登菲尔德

content_html_zh:
在人工智能行业，谷歌以自己看起来像房间里的成年人而自豪：安静、稳定、经过时间考验。 周三，即使该公司宣布了迄今为止最大规模的人工智能组织改组，谷歌及其领导者仍呈现出统一战线，将他们的信息集中在这些变化如何促进未来的成功上。

但现实情况是，一系列高管变动可能预示着谷歌人工智能组织内部存在更深层次的问题。 首先是它在人工智能竞赛中的脆弱地位，然后延伸到谷歌 DeepMind 领导者 Demis Hassabis 对长期研究而不是短期产品运输的兴趣，以及 DeepMind 首席科学家 Jeff Dean 等高层员工的政治反对等问题。

一名因担心遭到报复而要求匿名的谷歌现任员工表示，其中一个变化——迪恩的离职——是“谷歌理想主义的残余”完全消失的一个例子。 “失去杰夫将继续谷歌的人才流失，”他们说。 “很可能的结果就是平庸。”

周三的消息震动了人工智能行业，在人工智能研究人员像抢椅子游戏一样不断在角色和实验室之间切换的时代，这是很难做到的。 谷歌宣布 Demis Hassabis 将退出 DeepMind 的日常运营，专注于 AGI 和研究； DeepMind 现任首席技术官 Koray Kavukcuoglu 将接替 Hassabis 领导 DeepMind。 与此同时，在谷歌工作了 27 年的资深员工、公司第 30 名员工杰夫·迪恩 (Jeff Dean) 将与谷歌三名顶尖人工智能研究人员一起离开该组织，组建一家新的人工智能初创公司。

“失去杰夫将继续谷歌的人才流失。 平庸是可能的结果。”

谷歌被广泛认为是人工智能竞赛中最成功的老牌科技巨头，远远超过了 Meta、亚马逊和苹果。 但谷歌仍然被认为比 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 行动缓慢，而且它在前沿模型方面肯定没有超越它们。 哈萨比斯和谷歌首席执行官桑达尔·皮查伊都在声明中阐述了这一点。

皮查伊写道：“我们致力于走在前沿，并且非常专注于我们需要改进的领域。”他补充道，“我们必须继续快速行动，目标明确。” 哈萨比斯写道，该公司正在进入“下一个篇章”，并且它拥有“从这里开始的所有要素，我坚信我们会的。”

人工智能行业的关键人物似乎将这些变化视为哈萨比斯退到一边，转而支持以更快的速度、以产品为中心的 GDM 推进。

“谷歌的内部竞争比我在过去十年中看到的要激烈得多，主要是围绕人工智能产品领域，”一位最近离开公司并了解谷歌人工智能业务的前谷歌员工告诉 The Verge。 他们补充说，为了适应日益激烈的竞争，雇佣更多员工可以加快推出更多产品的压力很大。

“谷歌的内部竞争比我在过去十年中看到的要激烈得多，主要是围绕人工智能产品领域。”

人工智能行业内的另一位消息人士因与人工智能实验室持续合作而要求匿名，他表示：“我同意大家的看法，这是杰米斯失去影响力的标志。”

哈萨比斯并没有安静地表示，他的兴趣在于人工智能可能带来的科学进步，也许比该技术的商业化更重要。 皮查伊在一篇博客文章中写道，哈萨比斯的下一步行动将集中于作为 DeepMind 主席和 Alphabet 首席科学家“积极塑造 AGI 的未来”，同时继续领导药物发现衍生公司 Isomorphic Labs。

但人工智能领导力只是谷歌面临的问题之一——The Verge 采访的业内人士不断回到一个主要问题：这在多大程度上与谷歌内部日益加剧的道德冲突有关？

非营利性人工智能行业监管机构 The Midas Project 的创始人泰勒·约翰斯顿 (Tyler Johnston) 告诉 The Verge，哈萨比斯角色转变和 Dean 离职的一个因素可能是谷歌与国防部的协议。 该协议可能允许将谷歌人工智能用于大规模监视和致命自主武器。

约翰斯顿说：“这已经导致 DeepMind 员工离职和成立工会。” “有许多迹象表明迪恩和哈萨比斯个人可能感到反对。 事实上，DeepMind 最初被谷歌收购时签订了一项协议，不会出于军事或情报目的出售该技术。”

受到人工智能研究人员密切关注的博主兹维·莫肖维茨 (Zvi Mowshowitz) 也表示，迪恩的离职决定可能“与谷歌对 DoW 合同的决定有关”。

“DeepMind 最初被谷歌收购，并达成协议，不会出于军事或情报目的出售该技术。”

Dean 将离职并创立 Discovery Loop，这是一家人工智能初创公司，旨在自动化药物发现、硬件设计、清洁能源和材料设计等领域的数千个科学和工程实验。 与他一起作为联合创始人的还有另外三名顶尖的谷歌人工智能研究人员：Sanjay Ghemawat、Quoc Le 和 Oriol Vinyals。

“失去杰夫感觉就像是对谷歌内部道德和基本人类尊严的打击，”谷歌现任员工表示。 “他是这里为数不多的愿意就道德问题发表意见的可见、有权势的人物之一，例如 ICE 特工处决美国公民、人工智能监视和自主致命武器。”

在该公司坚守其人工智能军事用途的红线后，迪恩是国防部将人类标签列为供应链风险的最引人注目的反对者之一。 今年 3 月，迪恩是提交一份支持 Anthropic 诉讼的非当事人意见陈述的数十位科技行业领导者和员工之一，表达了对特朗普政府决定以及人工智能风险和影响的担忧。 （他还在 1 月份反驳了特朗普政府，称 ICE 杀害亚历克斯·普雷蒂“绝对可耻”，“每个人，无论政治派别，都应该谴责这一行为。”）

杰夫·迪恩（Jeff Dean）过去曾公开否认与 Anthropic 相同的两条红线。

今年 4 月，在 Anthropic 与国防部就其红线（禁止国内大规模监控和致命自主武器（没有人参与））进行了旷日持久的斗争之后，谷歌成为愉快地填补 Anthropic 五角大楼黑名单留下的空白的公司之一。 与其他几家公司一样，谷歌签署协议，允许五角大楼将其人工智能用于“任何合法用途”。

迪恩过去曾公开否认这两条红线。 今年二月，他在 X 上写道，“大规模监控违反了第四修正案，并对言论自由产生了寒蝉效应。 监控系统很容易被滥用于政治或歧视目的。” 2018 年，迪安和哈萨比斯都签署了一项公开承诺，否认致命的自主武器：“我们签名者同意，夺取人类生命的决定绝不应该委托给机器。”

因与五角大楼交易而辞职的谷歌研究员亚历克斯·特纳(Alex Turner)上个月在一篇专栏文章中写道，迪恩的“离职对公司来说将是一场灾难”，并且“通过签署[非当事人意见陈述]，他打破了公司的界限，这可能会让最高管理层内部的事情变得尴尬。”

在 Dean 今年早些时候签署的法庭之友简报中，该组织写道：“我们构建、训练和研究大规模人工智能系统，为广泛的用户和部署提供服务，包括在国家安全、执法和军事行动等重要领域。” 该组织将自己描述为“直接了解这些系统能做什么、不能做什么，以及当它们的部署超过旨在管理它们的法律和道德框架时会面临什么危险的专业人士。”

迪恩的离开可能会消除一位备受瞩目的批评者，但这肯定不会消除整个组织内部的批评。 今年以来，越来越多的谷歌员工表达了对该组织政治的不满。

“谢尔盖（布林）在政治上来了个 180 度转变，桑达尔在特朗普就职典礼上支持特朗普，”谷歌现任员工说道。 “现在，公司仅存的愿意就道德问题发声的人物之一已经离开了。 谁知道我们接下来会卖什么？”
